title: Water, impurities and hardness
learn: Natural water contains dissolved, suspended and biological impurities; its quality depends on the source and surroundings.
Hardness is mainly caused by dissolved salts of calcium and magnesium.
Hardness is expressed conveniently as calcium-carbonate equivalent and may be temporary or permanent.

sections.heading: Introduction: natural water and its sources
paragraphs: Water is one of nature’s most abundant and useful compounds. It is essential for life and is also widely used in industry, especially for steam generation, cooling, washing and processing.

Natural water is rarely pure. During its passage through the atmosphere and over or through the earth, it takes up suspended matter, dissolved salts, gases and microorganisms. The amount and nature of these impurities depend on the source of water.

book_refs.note: Introduction and natural sources of water

sections.heading: Impurities in natural water
paragraphs: Natural water may contain physical, chemical and biological impurities. Suspended matter causes turbidity; dissolved mineral matter includes salts of calcium, magnesium, sodium and iron; dissolved gases include oxygen and carbon dioxide; and biological impurities include microorganisms.
For engineering purposes, dissolved calcium and magnesium salts are especially important because they produce hardness.

sections.heading: Hardness of water
paragraphs: Hardness is the characteristic of water which prevents the lathering of soap. It is mainly due to dissolved bicarbonates, chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium.
Temporary or carbonate hardness is caused mainly by bicarbonates of calcium and magnesium. It can be removed by boiling.
Permanent or non-carbonate hardness is caused mainly by chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium. It cannot be removed by simple boiling.

sections.heading: Removal of temporary hardness by boiling
paragraphs: On boiling, bicarbonates of calcium and magnesium decompose and form insoluble precipitates. The precipitated matter can then be removed from the water.

sections.heading: Calcium-carbonate equivalents
paragraphs: Since hardness may be caused by several different salts, the amounts of the hardness-producing substances are converted into their calcium-carbonate equivalents before they are added.
The calcium-carbonate equivalent of a hardness-producing substance is the amount of CaCO₃ that is chemically equivalent to the given amount of that substance.
formulas: \(\text{CaCO}_3\text{ equivalent}=\dfrac{\text{mass of hardness-producing substance}\times 50}{\text{chemical equivalent of hardness-producing substance}}\)

tables.caption: CaCO₃ conversion factors
headers: Factor for conversion to CaCO₃ equivalent

sections.heading: Units and degree of hardness
paragraphs: Hardness is commonly expressed as parts per million (ppm), milligrams per litre (mg/L), degree Clark, degree French or milliequivalents per litre.
For dilute water, 1 mg/L of CaCO₃-equivalent hardness is numerically equal to 1 ppm.

self_checks.question: Why is hardness expressed as CaCO₃ equivalent?
self_checks.answer: It converts different hardness-producing salts to one common basis, making their contributions directly additive and comparable.

self_checks.question: Which type of hardness is removed by boiling?

title: Hardness calculations and complexometric estimation
learn: Convert each hardness-producing constituent into its CaCO₃ equivalent before calculating hardness.
In the EDTA method, Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ form stable complexes with EDTA.
At about pH 10, Eriochrome Black T gives a wine-red metal–indicator complex; the end point is a distinct blue colour.
Total, permanent and temporary hardness are obtained from the EDTA volumes used in the three titrations.

sections.heading: Numerical calculation of hardness from dissolved salts
paragraphs: For a water analysis containing several salts, first calculate the CaCO₃ equivalent of each hardness-producing constituent. Add the bicarbonate contributions for temporary hardness and the chloride and sulphate contributions for permanent hardness.
Total hardness is the sum of temporary and permanent hardness.

sections.heading: Example 4 — temporary and total hardness
paragraphs: Calculate the temporary and total hardness of a sample of water containing \(\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2}=73\,mg/L\), \(\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2}=162\,mg/L\), \(\mathrm{MgCl_2}=95\,mg/L\) and \(\mathrm{CaSO_4}=136\,mg/L\).

sections.heading: Principle of the EDTA complexometric method
paragraphs: The EDTA method is a complexometric method. Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), used in the form of its disodium salt, forms complex ions with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺.
Eriochrome Black T (EBT) is used as the indicator. At about pH 10, EBT forms an unstable wine-red complex with the hardness ions.

During titration, EDTA forms a more stable metal–EDTA complex. When nearly all Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions have been complexed, the next drop of EDTA releases EBT from the metal–indicator complex and the colour changes from wine red to distinct blue. This colour change marks the end point.

sections.heading: Preparation of solutions for the EDTA method
paragraphs: 1. Standard hard water: Dissolve 1.0 g of pure, dry CaCO₃ in the minimum quantity of dilute HCl. Evaporate to dryness on a water bath, dissolve the residue in distilled water and make the volume to 1 L. Each mL contains 1 mg of CaCO₃-equivalent hardness.
2. EDTA solution: Dissolve 4 g of pure EDTA crystals and 0.1 g of MgCl₂ in 1 L of distilled water.
3. Indicator: Dissolve 0.5 g of Eriochrome Black T in 100 mL of alcohol.
4. Buffer solution: Add 67.5 g of NH₄Cl to 570 mL of concentrated ammonia solution and dilute with distilled water to 1 L.

tables.caption: Preparation quantities for the hardness-by-EDTA method
rows: 1.0 g pure, dry CaCO₃; dissolve with minimum dilute HCl, evaporate to dryness, redissolve and make to 1 L; 1 mL corresponds to 1 mg CaCO₃ equivalent
4 g pure EDTA crystals + 0.1 g MgCl₂ in 1 L distilled water
0.5 g Eriochrome Black T in 100 mL alcohol
67.5 g NH₄Cl added to 570 mL concentrated ammonia solution, then diluted to 1 L

sections.heading: Standardisation of EDTA and titration of total hardness
paragraphs: 5. Standardisation of EDTA: Pipette 50 mL of standard hard water into a conical flask. Add 10–15 mL of buffer solution and 4–5 drops of indicator. Titrate with EDTA until the wine-red colour changes to clear blue. Let the volume of EDTA used be \(V_1\) mL.
6. Titration of unknown hard water: Titrate 50 mL of the water sample in the same way. Let the volume of EDTA used be \(V_2\) mL.

sections.heading: Permanent hardness and temporary hardness by EDTA
paragraphs: 7. Titration of permanent hardness: Take 250 mL of the water sample and boil it until the volume is reduced to about 50 mL. Filter off the precipitated CaCO₃ and Mg(OH)₂, wash the precipitate, collect the filtrate and washings in a 250 mL measuring flask, and make the volume up to 250 mL with distilled water.
Titrate 50 mL of this boiled-water sample in the same way. Let the volume of EDTA used be \(V_3\) mL.

sections.heading: Advantages of the EDTA method
paragraphs: The EDTA method is preferred because it gives greater accuracy, is convenient, and is more rapid.

self_checks.question: What colour change marks the EDTA hardness end point?
How are total and permanent hardness distinguished in the EDTA method?
self_checks.answer: Total hardness is measured directly on the sample; permanent hardness is measured after boiling, filtering and restoring the sample volume. Temporary hardness is total minus permanent hardness.

title: Boiler troubles: scales and sludges
learn: Sludge is a soft, loose and slimy precipitate; scale is a hard, adherent deposit on the inner boiler surface.
Scale wastes fuel, lowers boiler safety and efficiency, and may lead to explosion.
Scale and sludge are controlled by suitable external and internal treatment of boiler water.

sections.heading: Scale and sludge formation in boilers
paragraphs: In a boiler, dissolved salts become more concentrated as water is converted into steam. When their solubility is exceeded, they separate from the water as deposits.
Sludges are soft, loose and slimy precipitates which do not form a hard adhering coating on the boiler surface. Scales are hard deposits which adhere firmly to the inner walls of the boiler.

figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 1, Scale and sludge in boilers, on textbook page 7.

sections.heading: Disadvantages of sludge formation
paragraphs: Sludges are poor conductors of heat and therefore waste heat. They may also choke pipes and other fittings and disturb the working of the boiler.
Sludges are generally removed by frequent blow-down operation.

sections.heading: Causes of scale formation
paragraphs: Scale formation may result from decomposition of bicarbonates, decrease in the solubility of calcium sulphate at high temperature, hydrolysis of magnesium salts, and the presence of silica.
bullets: Decomposition of bicarbonates: \(\mathrm{Ca(HCO_3)_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3\downarrow + H_2O + CO_2\uparrow}\).
Deposition of calcium sulphate: the solubility of \(\mathrm{CaSO_4}\) decreases at boiler temperatures, so it can precipitate directly as a hard deposit.
Hydrolysis of magnesium salts: dissolved magnesium salts can hydrolyse and precipitate \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}\), contributing to scale.
Silica and silicates: silica may form calcium or magnesium silicate deposits, which are particularly hard and firmly adherent.

sections.heading: Disadvantages of scale formation
paragraphs: 1. Wastage of fuel: Scale has low thermal conductivity, so heat transfer to the boiler water decreases and more fuel is required.
2. Lowering of boiler safety: Overheating makes boiler tubes softer and weaker and may distort them, especially in high-pressure boilers.
3. Decrease in efficiency: Scale may deposit in valves and condensers and partially choke them.
4. Danger of explosion: If a thick scale cracks, water may suddenly come in contact with overheated metal and produce a large quantity of steam.

tables.caption: Effect of scale thickness on fuel wastage

sections.heading: Prevention of scale and sludge
paragraphs: Scale formation can be prevented by external treatment, in which hardness-producing constituents are removed from feed water, and by internal treatment, in which suitable chemicals are added directly to the boiler water.
In internal treatment, scale-forming impurities are either precipitated as loose sludge removable by blow-down or converted into soluble compounds which remain in water.

book_refs.note: Boiler scale, sludge, causes and effects

self_checks.question: What is the main physical difference between scale and sludge?
self_checks.answer: Scale is hard and adherent; sludge is soft, loose and non-adherent.

title: Internal treatment of boiler feed water
learn: Colloidal conditioning produces non-sticky, loose deposits that can be removed by blow-down.
Phosphate conditioning converts hardness into soft calcium and magnesium phosphate sludge.
Calgon conditioning prevents scale and sludge by forming soluble complexes with calcium salts.

sections.heading: Internal treatment: principle
paragraphs: Internal treatment is carried out by adding a suitable chemical directly to the boiler water. The reagent either converts scale-forming impurities into loose sludge, removable by blow-down, or converts them into soluble compounds which do not form scale.

sections.heading: Colloidal conditioning
paragraphs: In low-pressure boilers, scale formation can be avoided by adding organic substances such as kerosene, tannin and agar-agar. These substances coat the scale-forming precipitates and produce non-sticky, loose deposits which can be removed by blow-down.

sections.heading: Phosphate conditioning
paragraphs: In high-pressure boilers, sodium phosphate is added to react with hardness-producing salts and form soft, non-adherent sludge of calcium and magnesium phosphates. The sludge can be removed by blow-down.

The main phosphates used are sodium dihydrogen phosphate (acidic), disodium hydrogen phosphate (weakly alkaline) and trisodium phosphate (alkaline). The choice depends on the alkalinity of the boiler-feed water.

sections.heading: Calgon conditioning
paragraphs: Calgon conditioning consists of adding Calgon, sodium hexametaphosphate \(\mathrm{(NaPO_3)_6}\), to boiler water. It prevents scale and sludge formation by forming a soluble complex with calcium salts.

book_refs.note: Internal treatment methods required by R25

title: External treatment: ion-exchange demineralisation
learn: Ion-exchange resins exchange their mobile ions with ions present in water.
Cation-exchange resin replaces cations such as Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ by H⁺; anion-exchange resin replaces anions by OH⁻.
The released H⁺ and OH⁻ combine to form water, giving demineralised water.
Exhausted resins are regenerated and reused.

sections.heading: Ion-exchange or deionisation process
paragraphs: Ion-exchange resins are insoluble, cross-linked polymeric materials containing ionisable functional groups. They exchange their mobile ions with ions present in the water passing through them.
Demineralisation is carried out by passing water first through a cation-exchange resin in the H⁺ form and then through an anion-exchange resin in the OH⁻ form.

sections.heading: Cation-exchange resin
paragraphs: Cation-exchange resins contain acidic functional groups and exchange H⁺ ions for cations such as Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺. Thus the dissolved salts are converted into the corresponding acids.

figures.figure_name: Acidic or cation exchange resin (sulphonate form)
figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 6, Acidic or cation exchange resin (sulphonate form), on textbook page 17.

sections.heading: Anion-exchange resin
paragraphs: Anion-exchange resins contain basic functional groups and exchange OH⁻ ions for anions such as Cl⁻ and SO₄²⁻. The H⁺ released by the cation exchanger combines with the OH⁻ released by the anion exchanger to form water.

figures.figure_name: Basic or anion exchange resin (hydroxide form)
figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 7, Basic or anion exchange resin (hydroxide form), on textbook page 18.

sections.heading: Demineralisation plant
paragraphs: Hard water is passed through the cation exchanger and then through the anion exchanger. The outgoing water is deionised or demineralised and contains only a very small amount of dissolved salts.

figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 8, Demineralisation of water, on textbook page 19.

sections.heading: Regeneration of exhausted ion exchangers
paragraphs: The exhausted cation-exchange resin is regenerated with dilute mineral acid and then washed with deionised water.
The exhausted anion-exchange resin is regenerated with dilute NaOH solution and then washed. The regenerated resins are ready for reuse.
In a mixed-bed exchanger, the cation and anion resins are separated for regeneration and mixed again before use.

figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 9, Regeneration of mixed-bed ion exchanger, on textbook page 20.

sections.heading: Advantages and limitations
paragraphs: Ion exchange produces water of very low residual hardness and is suitable for demineralisation. The plant is compact and the resins can be regenerated.
Turbid water should be clarified before ion exchange because suspended matter can clog the resin bed.

self_checks.question: What ions are released by the cation and anion exchangers?
self_checks.answer: The cation exchanger releases H⁺; the anion exchanger releases OH⁻.

title: Potable water and municipal treatment
learn: Potable water should be clear, pleasant, reasonably soft and free from harmful microorganisms and objectionable impurities.
Municipal treatment removes suspended and colloidal matter by screening, sedimentation, coagulation and filtration.
Disinfection destroys disease-producing microorganisms; chlorination and break-point chlorination are important methods.

sections.heading: Drinking or municipal water: requirements
paragraphs: Drinking or potable water is water fit for human consumption. It should be sparkling clear and odourless, pleasant in taste, reasonably cool, low in turbidity, free from objectionable dissolved gases and harmful minerals, reasonably soft, and free from disease-producing microorganisms.
Important quality limits are shown below.

sections.heading: Sequence of municipal-water treatment
paragraphs: Natural surface water does not satisfy all the requirements of drinking water. For domestic use, the principal treatment operations are removal of suspended impurities followed by disinfection.

sections.heading: Screening and sedimentation
paragraphs: Screening: Raw water is passed through screens having a large number of holes so that floating matter is retained.
Sedimentation: Water is allowed to stand undisturbed in large tanks so that most suspended particles settle under gravity. The clear supernatant water is then drawn off.

sections.heading: Coagulation
paragraphs: Fine suspended and colloidal impurities are removed by sedimentation with coagulation. A suitable coagulant is added before sedimentation.
The coagulant forms an insoluble gelatinous floc which adsorbs and entangles very fine suspended particles and forms larger flocs that settle readily. Alum and sodium aluminate are common coagulants.

sections.heading: Filtration through a sand filter
paragraphs: After sedimentation and coagulation, water is passed through a sand filter. Fine suspended matter is retained in the pores of the sand bed, giving clearer water before disinfection.

figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 10, Sand filter, on textbook page 21.

sections.heading: Disinfection by chlorination
paragraphs: Even after sedimentation, coagulation and filtration, water may contain pathogenic microorganisms. Disinfection is the process of destroying disease-producing microorganisms and making water safe for use.

Chlorine is widely used for disinfection. In water it forms hypochlorous acid, which is mainly responsible for the germicidal action. Chlorine should be thoroughly mixed with the water and allowed sufficient contact time.

figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 11, Chlorinator, on textbook page 23.

sections.heading: Break-point chlorination
paragraphs: When chlorine is added to water, it is first consumed by reducing substances and by the formation of chlorine compounds. With further addition, these compounds are destroyed and the residual chlorine falls to a minimum.

The point at which the chlorine demand is satisfied and free residual chlorine begins to appear is called the break point. Beyond this point, further addition of chlorine gives an increasing free residual chlorine concentration.

figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 12, Break-point chlorination curve, on textbook page 24.

sections.heading: Overall drinking-water treatment plant
paragraphs: A drinking-water treatment plant combines the main purification operations in sequence, from the intake of raw water to the delivery of treated water.

figures.figure_name: Flow diagram of drinking water treatment plant
figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 14, Flow diagram of drinking water treatment plant, on textbook page 25.

cautions: Use the drinking-water specifications stated in this section.

self_checks.question: What is break-point chlorination?
self_checks.answer: It is the stage at which chlorine demand has been satisfied and further chlorine addition begins to produce a free residual chlorine concentration.

title: Membrane separation and reverse osmosis
learn: Microfiltration, ultrafiltration and nanofiltration are R25 membrane-separation topics.
Reverse osmosis is used for desalination of brackish or saline water.
In reverse osmosis, pressure greater than the osmotic pressure forces water through a semipermeable membrane in the reverse direction of normal osmosis.

sections.heading: Desalination of brackish water: reverse osmosis
paragraphs: Reverse osmosis is used for desalination of brackish or saline water. In normal osmosis, solvent passes through a semipermeable membrane from the dilute solution to the concentrated solution.

If a pressure greater than the osmotic pressure is applied on the concentrated side, the direction of solvent flow is reversed. Water is forced through the semipermeable membrane while dissolved salts are retained on the high-pressure side.

figures.alt: Placeholder for textbook Fig. 17, Reverse osmosis cell, on textbook page 27.

sections.heading: Advantages of reverse osmosis
paragraphs: Reverse osmosis is a compact and comparatively simple process. It can be operated continuously and does not require a phase change of water, so its energy requirement is lower than evaporation-based desalination.

self_checks.question: What pressure condition is required for reverse osmosis?
self_checks.answer: An applied pressure greater than the osmotic pressure on the concentrated/saline side.
